candidates.teaser: Sharks existed before trees — and that changes everything you thought you knew about ancient Earth.
candidates.video_title: Sharks Are Older Than Trees (This Is Wild)
candidates.video_description: Sharks have roamed Earth's oceans for over 450 million years — nearly 90 million years before the first tree ever grew. While sharks evolved and thrived, trees hadn't even been invented by nature yet. This fact quietly rewrites how we picture prehistoric Earth.
candidates.script: Sharks were already ancient by the time the first tree appeared on Earth. Sharks have existed for 450 million years. Trees? Only 360 million. That means for 90 million years, sharks hunted in oceans on a planet with no forests, no leaves, no shade — just bare rock and open water. The ocean had apex predators before land had plants. So next time someone calls sharks primitive — they outlived almost everything that came after them.

candidates.topic: A day on Venus is longer than its year
candidates.teaser: On one planet in our solar system, a single day lasts longer than an entire year — and it spins backwards.
candidates.video_title: On Venus, a Day Is Longer Than a Year
candidates.video_description: Venus rotates so slowly on its axis that a single Venusian day lasts 243 Earth days — yet it completes a full orbit around the Sun in just 225 days. That means its day is longer than its year. Even stranger, it spins in the opposite direction to most planets.
candidates.script: On Venus, the sun rises in the west and sets in the east — because the planet spins backwards. But here's the part that breaks your brain: one day on Venus lasts 243 Earth days. Its orbit around the Sun? Only 225 days. That means a single day there is longer than an entire year. You could celebrate New Year before you even finish breakfast. How is that even physically possible?

candidates.topic: The inventor of the lobotomy won a Nobel Prize
candidates.teaser: A doctor received the Nobel Prize for a procedure that destroyed thousands of minds — and it was considered a breakthrough.
candidates.video_title: The Nobel Prize Winner Who Destroyed Brains
candidates.video_description: In 1949, António Egas Moniz won the Nobel Prize in Medicine for inventing the lobotomy — a surgery that severed connections in the brain's frontal lobe. Over 40,000 Americans alone underwent the procedure, many left permanently damaged. The prize has never been revoked.
candidates.script: In 1949, a doctor won the Nobel Prize in Medicine for drilling into people's skulls and cutting their brain apart. António Egas Moniz invented the lobotomy — a procedure performed on over 40,000 Americans, including children. Patients were left unable to feel emotion, make decisions, or live independently. The Nobel committee called it a landmark achievement. That prize has never been taken back. Does a discovery that ruins 40,000 lives deserve the world's highest honor?

candidates.topic: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
candidates.teaser: Cleopatra and the Moon landing have something in common that no one ever tells you about the pyramids.
candidates.video_title: Cleopatra Was Closer to the Moon Landing Than the Pyramids
candidates.video_description: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC. Cleopatra lived around 30 BC — making her 2,500 years removed from the pyramids. The Moon landing happened in 1969, just roughly 2,000 years after Cleopatra. She was chronologically closer to Armstrong's footstep than to the pharaohs who built Giza.
candidates.script: Cleopatra never saw the pyramids as ancient ruins — to her, they already were. The Great Pyramid was built in 2560 BC. Cleopatra lived in 30 BC. That's a 2,500-year gap between her and the builders of Giza. The Moon landing? 1969 AD — only about 2,000 years after Cleopatra. She was closer in time to Neil Armstrong stepping on the Moon than to the people who raised the pyramids. History isn't a straight line — it's a loop.

candidates.topic: Humans glow in the dark — just too faint to see
candidates.teaser: Your body is emitting light right now — not metaphorically, literally — and scientists have captured it on camera.
candidates.video_title: Your Body Glows in the Dark (You Just Can't See It)
candidates.video_description: The human body emits biophotons — actual visible light particles — produced by chemical reactions in our cells. The glow is roughly 1,000 times too dim for the naked eye to detect. In 2009, Japanese scientists used ultra-sensitive cameras to photograph this human glow for the first time, revealing it fluctuates throughout the day.
candidates.script: Your body is glowing right now. Not heat — actual light. Human cells produce biophotons, real visible-spectrum light particles, as a byproduct of chemical reactions. In 2009, Japanese scientists used cameras 1,000 times more sensitive than the human eye and photographed people in complete darkness — glowing faintly, brightest in the afternoon, dimming at night. Every person in this room is a slow, silent light source. The only reason you can't see it is that your eyes aren't sensitive enough.
